deep.reconstruction:
Context (§88–89): water flows from a large vessel, height a, through an inclined cylindrical tube of length b and square cross-section gg (so g is a side length). The tube makes angle ζ with the vertical, so cos ζ is the sine of its slope. Euler's friction law makes the friction force proportional to the pressure, with coefficient α and with l the water-column height of the atmosphere. For a wide, shallow vessel the velocity head is v = [a𝔅 + (1/α)(1−𝔅) g cos ζ − (1−𝔅) l] / [1 − (1−𝔅)𝔤], where 𝔅 = e^{−αb/g}. The denominator is positive, so there is flow only if the numerator is positive.

§90: Let a → 0. Flow then requires g cos ζ/α > l, i.e. sin(slope) > αl/g. Euler takes αl = 0.0075 ft (consistent with l ≈ 30 ft, α ≈ 1/4000). Writing g = nαl, the condition becomes sin(slope) > 1/n. So if n ≤ 1, i.e. g ≤ αl, there is no flow at any slope (sine ≤ 1).

§91: Euler transfers this to rivers, reading g as the river depth. Let the bed drop z ft per 1000 ft, so the sine of the slope is z/1000. With αl = 3/400 ft the condition is z/1000 > 3/(400g), i.e. z > 7.5/g = 1000αl/g. Below this critical slope the water would stand still.

§92: Euler announces a table of this critical slope against depth. The table is on the next page and is just z = 7.5/g, with slope × depth constant. The point of the page is a criterion for the onset of river flow, derived from Euler's pressure-proportional (Coulomb-type) model of fluid friction.
errors: §90 prints the condition as 'g cos ζ < αl'. From the numerator of §89 with a → 0, and from Euler's own paraphrase ('sinus decliuitatis maior … quam αl/g'), it must be g cos ζ > αl. The '<' is a misprint or slip.
§90: 'cos ζ > g/n' (as printed or transcribed) should be cos ζ > 1/n, since αl/g = 1/n. Euler states 1/n correctly a few lines later.

Modelling gap: in the pipe model gg is the area and the wetted perimeter is 4g, so the relevant length (area/perimeter) is g/4. For a wide open channel the analogous quantity is about the depth. Identifying g with river depth therefore shifts the critical slope by a constant factor. The open-channel transfer is heuristic: it carries over a closed-pipe formula including atmospheric pressure on all walls.

Physical error, inherent to the friction law: a Newtonian liquid has no threshold slope, since any slope produces flow. The predicted stagnation of rivers below z = 7.5/g ft per 1000 ft is false. A 15 ft deep river would need a fall of 0.5 ft per 1000 ft, while many large rivers flow on much smaller slopes.

The consequences on the next page are also unphysical: velocity grows exponentially with reach length, and flow speeds up when atmospheric pressure falls. They show the pressure-proportional friction hypothesis fails. This contrasts with Chézy's uniform-flow relation (v ∝ √(RS), 1768–1775).

Arithmetic check: 3/400 = 0.0075 is correct, and z > 3000/(400g) = 30/(4g) = 7.5/g is correct. The table values (15, 7.5, 5, 3.75, …, 1.87, 1.07, 0.94, 0.83, 0.68, 0.62, 0.58, 0.535, 0.50) all agree with 7.5/g to rounding.

ideas.what: Flow-onset (threshold) condition from a friction law proportional to pressure: no flow unless g·sin(slope) > αl.
ideas.modern_name: Yield/threshold criterion. Mathematically the same as the critical-thickness condition ρ g h sin θ > τ_y for a Bingham (yield-stress) layer on an incline.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Yield-stress fluids: Schwedoff (1890), Bingham (1916–1922). Coulomb friction: Amontons/Coulomb.
ideas.where_published: E260 itself, Novi Commentarii Acad. Petrop. 6 (1756/57, publ. 1761). Euler's pressure-proportional friction hypothesis in this memoir is discussed in Truesdell's introductions to Opera omnia II.12/13 (details unsure).

ideas.what: Critical slope of a river bed as a function of depth, with slope × depth = constant (z = 1000αl/g ft per 1000 ft), and a numerical table.
ideas.modern_name: Critical slope for a viscoplastic sheet flow (S_c = τ_y/(ρ g h)); no counterpart for Newtonian open-channel flow.
ideas.usually_credited_to: No accepted counterpart for water. For mudflows and lava: Johnson (1970), Coussot and others.
ideas.where_published: E260 §§91–92 and the table on p. 373.

ideas.what: Transfer of a closed inclined-pipe result to open-channel river flow, with tube side g read as depth.
ideas.modern_name: Hydraulic-radius analogy between pipe and channel flow.

missed.claim: Euler's pressure-proportional friction, with the atmospheric head l dominating, acts as a constant wall shear stress. It therefore yields exactly the yield-stress critical-depth law S_c·h = const = τ_y/(ρg), the same law now used for Bingham mudflows, lava and debris flows. Euler's threshold table is thus formally the first tabulated critical slope–thickness relation for a yield-stress layer on an incline, though he wrongly applied it to water. I am not aware of commentary that frames E260 this way. It is a historical curiosity rather than a usable result.
missed.quote: vt ergo aqua in alueo defluat, oportet sit z>30/(4g), seu z>1000αl/g
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historiographical: it shows an 18th-century friction law whose mathematics anticipates viscoplastic threshold flow. It has no new mathematical content for specialists.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a straightforward specialization of the preceding formula, with a minor sign misprint. The only notable point is the formal identity between Euler's (physically wrong) Coulomb-type threshold for river flow and the modern yield-stress critical-slope law. That is an interesting connection but not a hidden result.
transcription_corrections: §90: the printed 'g cos ζ < αl' matches the image but is a misprint in the original; the sense requires '>'.
§90: 'cos.ζ > g/n' should read cos.ζ > 1/n. The small fraction in the scan is consistent with 1/n, and the text later says 'quam 1/n'.
§91: '30/(4g)' is correct as printed; it equals 7.5/g.
